target.text: No official target exists for this composite risk index - it's designed to identify relative risk, not track progress against a threshold. Lower scores indicate lower risk of digital exclusion.

source.name: Digital Exclusion Risk Index (DERI) v1.5 - Greater Manchester Combined Authority
source.notes: The GLA/LOTI 'Mapping Digital Exclusion' dataset previously cited as the intended source for this indicator is genuinely limited to its five pilot boroughs (Barnet, Brent, Kensington & Chelsea, Southwark, Westminster) - Lewisham isn't covered, and no Lewisham-specific output has been published from it, confirmed via the London Datastore and LOTI's own project pages. GMCA's Digital Exclusion Risk Index (DERI) does cover every LSOA in England, Scotland and Wales, so Ladywell's 7 constituent LSOAs (E01003273/274/275/276/278/279/291, confirmed via ONS's official LSOA-to-ward best-fit lookup) are all scored. 2.5 is the population-weighted average of those 7 LSOAs' individual DERI scores, using DERI's Great-Britain-normalised variant (England IMD basis) - the only one of DERI's three normalisation options (local authority / nation / Great Britain) that's comparable across different areas, per GMCA's own methodology guide. Scores range from 2.06 to 3.18 across the 7 LSOAs, i.e. genuine within-ward variation rather than a flat borough figure. Ladywell's score sits toward the low end of the 0-10 scale, consistent with Trust for London's own commentary that 'much of London, due to its relatively young demographic and good broadband access, is in the lower range' nationally. Caveat: DERI is a composite built from 11 proxy indicators (deprivation, demography, broadband access) across three domains, not a direct survey of who's actually offline, and several of its components are dated - 'no qualifications', 'social grade' and 'day-to-day activities limited' all come from Census 2011, while IMD is 2019-based and broadband/unemployment/pension-credit data is from 2019-2021. GMCA's in-progress v2.0 rebuild moves to 2021 Census data but has not yet published a scored output, and the repo's latest release (v1.6, November 2022) publishes no LSOA-level scores file, so v1.5 remains the latest version with usable LSOA scores. The previous indicator here - GLA's 2022 estimate of ~270,000 Londoners completely offline (London-wide, not Lewisham-specific) - is kept as descriptive context below rather than as the snapshot, since it measures something DERI doesn't (an absolute headcount rather than a relative risk score).

TfL refreshed its PTAL toolkit to 'WebCAT 3.0' in 2025, updating scores from a 2015 baseline (with an interim 2019 borough-level PDF release for Lewisham) to reflect network changes since, including the Elizabeth line. source.notes: No Lewisham- or borough-level wealth distribution figure exists (the underlying ONS Wealth and Assets Survey - WAS - is not designed to produce reliable local authority estimates), so this uses the GLA's London-wide figure instead, labelled accordingly: households in the bottom half of London's wealth distribution hold just 4% of the capital's total household wealth, while the richest 10% of households hold over 60%. Underlying source: ONS Wealth and Assets Survey microdata, as analysed by the GLA's Economic Fairness programme. An older Trust for London page (trustforlondon.org.uk/data/wealth-distribution/, now archived and no longer updated) put the same England-wide poorest-50%-wealth-share at 9% and London's bottom-half share at 6.8%, using 2018-2020 WAS data - the GLA's 4% figure is treated as the more current reference here, but the two aren't a clean like-for-like trend (different WAS rounds/methodology), so no trend array is given rather than implying a precise year-on-year decline. Caveat: the Office for Statistics Regulation removed WAS's Official Statistics accreditation in June 2025, saying it was 'no longer of sufficient value or quality to meet users' needs' - treat this figure as broadly indicative of London's wealth concentration, not a precise measurement. This session's WebFetch/curl tools were blocked for both trustforlondon.org.uk and ons.gov.uk, so the exact WAS survey round behind the GLA's 4% figure could not be independently confirmed.

source.name: GLA London Datastore - Economic Fairness: Gender Pay Gap
source.notes: No Lewisham-specific gender pay gap figure was found for borough residents (ONS does publish ASHE Table 8, a residence-based earnings-by-local-authority dataset, which in principle could be used to derive one, but this session's tools could not reach ons.gov.uk to extract it - WebFetch and direct curl were both blocked by the environment's egress policy). This uses the GLA's London-wide figure instead: female employees in London were paid 14% less per hour than male employees on average in 2023 (mean hourly pay, all employees). Underlying source: ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE). Only this single year's figure could be confirmed via search; the GLA's own page reportedly notes the London gap 'has not fallen over more than a decade' unlike the national trend, but exact values for other years were not retrievable this session, so no fabricated trend is given - see Confidence.LOW.

local_social.indicator: Ethnicity pay gap (median hourly pay, White vs ethnic minority employees)

source.name: GLA London Datastore - Economic Fairness: Ethnicity Pay Gap
source.notes: No Lewisham-specific ethnicity pay gap figure exists at borough level (sample sizes in ONS's source surveys are too small to support reliable local authority breakdowns by ethnicity), so this uses London-wide figures. The GLA states the gap in median hourly pay between White and Black/Asian/minority ethnic employees in London is 'more than 22%' (most recent, based on the ONS Annual Population Survey), against roughly 1% across England & Wales outside London - London has consistently had the largest regional ethnicity pay gap in the country. Trend points for 2018 (21.7%) and 2019 (23.8%) are from ONS's own annual 'Ethnicity pay gaps in Great Britain' regional bulletins (unadjusted/raw gap, London region); the current point uses 22.0 as a conservative reading of the GLA's 'more than 22%' statement since an exact decimal for the latest year could not be confirmed - WebFetch/curl access to data.london.gov.uk and ons.gov.uk was blocked in this session, so this is built from search-result summaries rather than the primary tables directly. Treat the three points as broadly indicative of a persistently large, fairly stable gap rather than a precise year-on-year series.

source.name: Trussell - End of Year Stats (Local Authority data)
source.notes: Lewisham's Trussell-network foodbanks distributed 22,476 emergency parcels in 2025 (14,961 for adults, 7,515 for children) across 7 locations - down 12% from a 2023 peak of 25,659, but still more than triple 2018's 7,311. Trussell switched from financial-year to calendar-year reporting in this release; data pulled directly from its 'Local authority' breakdown sheet (eys_2025_parcel_stats.xlsx, published March 2026). Counts parcels given out by Trussell-affiliated foodbanks only - excludes independent food banks and social supermarkets (e.g. Evelyn Community Store, see Get Involved) that aren't part of the Trussell network, so it understates total local food-aid demand. Replaces the previous indicator here (OHID Fingertips 'moderate to severe food insecurity' modelled risk measure, indicator 93864), which had only two years published (2021, 2022) with no newer round in sight - this dataset is genuinely local-authority level and updates annually.

source.name: OHID National Dental Epidemiology Programme (NDEP) - oral health surveys of 5-year-olds and Year 6 children
source.notes: Headline and chart show Reception (5-year-olds) only: 18.90% in 2023/24, the most recent round, surveyed roughly every 2 years since 2007/08 with a well-established Lewisham time series. Year 6 has only ever been surveyed once nationally (9.90%, academic year 2022/23) - no repeat round exists yet, so it has no trend to chart and isn't blended into the headline figure (an earlier version averaged the two ages into an artificial 14.40%, which matched neither age group's own number nor the Reception-only chart - see 'what this measures' below for both figures stated separately). England averages for the same rounds: Reception 22.4%, Year 6 16.15% - Lewisham runs below England and well below the London average (27.4% Reception, 2024) on both age groups. Direct extraction of the official NDEP 2023/24 round results (UTLA table) ranks Lewisham's 18.9% as the 6th-lowest of 32 London boroughs (tied with Bromley) that round - corrects an earlier, unverifiable claim sourced to an NHS South East London ICB presentation that cited '4th-lowest of 33 boroughs', which could not be traced to a genuine 33-borough comparison (the only '4th-lowest' ranking found was among a 6-borough South East London ICB subset, not all London boroughs).

local_social.indicator: % of people over 17 years old with type 2 diabetes

source.name: OHID Fingertips Diabetes Profile - QOF prevalence, 17+
source.notes: 7.22% of Lewisham residents aged 17+ had diabetes recorded on GP disease registers in 2024/25 (QOF prevalence), up from 5.67% in 2012/13. This QOF measure records all diagnosed diabetes (type 1 and type 2 combined); type 2 accounts for around 90% of diagnosed cases nationally. A type-2-only measure (National Diabetes Audit) is published only at South East London ICB level (covering Lewisham, Southwark, Lambeth, Greenwich, Bromley and Bexley together), where it stood at 6.35% in 2024/25 - consistent with Lewisham's QOF figure once the ~90% type-2 share is applied. Lewisham has run significantly below the England average (7.89% in 2024/25) throughout this series, and is now almost identical to the London average (7.22% in 2024/25, re-pulled directly from the Fingertips API 2026-10-31 - supersedes an earlier 7.08% figure, a genuine data revision between pulls, not an error in either).
